definition: An 8-ping/8-position connector used primarily for Ethernet networking.
Resolves human-readable hostnames (e.g., google.com) to IP addresses. Uses Port 53.
Small Outline Dual In-line Memory Module. A compact memory form factor used in laptops, roughly half the physical length of desktop DIMMs.
Zero Insertion Force connector. A ribbon cable connector that uses a locking latch to secure thin flex cables without requiring force.
Creating a sector-by-sector duplicate of a hard drive onto another drive, preserving the OS, applications, and settings.
DDR4 SO-DIMMs use 260 pins for laptop memory modules.
DDR5 SO-DIMMs use 262 pins for laptop memory modules.
A wireless card form factor measuring 22mm wide by 30mm long, commonly used for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules in laptops.
A miniature coaxial connector used to connect antenna cables to internal wireless cards in laptops.
Devices that measure biological characteristics (fingerprints, facial recognition) to authenticate user access to secure systems.
Microsoft's biometric authentication system using Infrared (IR) cameras for facial recognition, works regardless of ambient lighting.
A built-in proximity scanner in laptops that enables tap-to-authenticate functionality using employee smart badges and security tokens.
A physical optical screen or electronic toggle (e.g., HP Sure View) that narrows viewing angles to defeat visual eavesdropping or 'shoulder surfing'.
The primary battery technology used in modern internal laptop batteries, secured by screws under the chassis cover.
A chemical degradation condition in batteries that indicates they pose a fire/explosion risk and must be disposed of according to environmental and hazardous waste guidelines.
A display technology using liquid crystal solution sandwiched between polarizing filters; requires an external LED backlight to produce visible images.
LCD panel where crystals align horizontally; offers excellent color accuracy and wide 178° viewing angles, used in professional graphics displays.
LCD panel where crystals twist as current passes; offers fast response times and low cost, but poor color accuracy and narrow viewing angles.
LCD panel where crystals align vertically when unpowered; offers deep black levels and high contrast, but slower response times than TN panels.
Self-illuminating display technology where each pixel generates its own light; provides true blacks, superior contrast, and requires no separate backlight.
The transparent glass layer bonded to the front of a display panel that translates touch or stylus input into digital coordinates.
A high-voltage component used in legacy CCFL-backlit LCD screens to convert DC power to AC power. Modern LED displays do not require inverters.
Display technology (like OLED) where each pixel generates its own light without requiring a background backlight source.
A permanent performance degradation in OLED displays caused by static images displayed at high brightness for extended periods.
Connection-oriented, reliable transport layer protocol that uses a 3-way handshake and guarantees packet delivery in sequence order.
Connectionless, lightweight transport layer protocol designed for speed; delivers packets on a 'best effort' basis without guarantees or retransmission.
The TCP process to establish a connection: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, which must complete before data transfer begins.
TCP port 80 protocol that transfers unencrypted web pages across the World Wide Web.
TCP port 443 protocol that encrypts web traffic using TLS/SSL to secure sensitive web browsing and transactions.
TCP port 22 protocol providing encrypted remote terminal connection for secure CLI administrative access.
TCP port 23 legacy protocol for unencrypted remote terminal access; transmits credentials and commands in plain text (insecure).
TCP ports 20/21 protocol for transmitting files between client and server. Port 21 manages commands; Port 20 handles data transfer.
TCP port 445 protocol used by Windows for sharing files, folders, and printers across a local network.
TCP port 548 legacy proprietary file sharing protocol used by macOS devices.
TCP port 25 protocol that sends email from clients to servers or transfers mail between email servers.
TCP port 110 protocol that downloads email from a server to a single local device, typically deleting it from the server afterwards.
TCP port 143 protocol that synchronizes email across multiple devices while keeping mail stored on the central server.
UDP ports 67/68 protocol that automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS servers to network clients.
UDP ports 161/162 protocol that monitors and gathers metrics from network devices. Queries use UDP 161; traps use UDP 162.
TCP port 389 protocol that queries and manages directory services like Microsoft Active Directory for network authentication.
TCP port 636 protocol that encrypts LDAP directory traffic over SSL/TLS.
TCP port 3389 Microsoft proprietary protocol enabling graphical view and remote control of a Windows desktop PC.
UDP ports 137/138, TCP port 139 legacy Windows protocol suite for hostname resolution, datagram services, and session handling.
Legacy Ethernet cable supporting maximum 100 Mbps over 100 meters at 100 MHz frequency.
Enhanced Ethernet cable supporting 1 Gbps (1000 Mbps) over 100 meters at 100 MHz frequency, standard for home and small office networks.
Ethernet cable supporting 10 Gbps up to 55 meters or 1 Gbps up to 100 meters at 250 MHz, includes internal plastic separator (spline).
Augmented Ethernet cable supporting 10 Gbps up to 100 meters at 500 MHz frequency, used in enterprise 10-Gigabit Ethernet networks.
Standard network cable without internal foil shielding; highly flexible and cost-effective but susceptible to strong external EMI.
Network cable with internal foil wrapping around wire pairs; shields against heavy electromagnetic interference in industrial environments.
8-position, 8-conductor (8P8C) modular connector used for Ethernet network cabling.
6-position, 2-conductor (or 4-conductor) modular connector used for telephone lines and DSL modems.
Threaded coaxial cable connector used for cable TV and cable internet modems with RG-6 or RG-59 cabling.
Ethernet pinout standard: White/Green, Green, White/Orange, Blue, White/Blue, Orange, White/Brown, Brown.
Ethernet pinout standard: White/Orange, Orange, White/Green, Blue, White/Blue, Green, White/Brown, Brown.
Ethernet cable using same standard (T568A or T568B) on both ends; connects unlike devices (e.g., PC to Switch).
Ethernet cable using T568A on one end and T568B on the other; connects like devices (e.g., PC to PC). Modern devices support Auto-MDIX.
Fiber-optic cable with narrow core diameter (~9 microns) using laser light; supports exceptional distances (tens of kilometers) for WAN backbones.
Fiber-optic cable with larger core diameter (~50-62.5 microns) using LED; supports shorter distances (up to ~500 meters) for LAN backbones.
Round, bayonet-style twist-and-lock fiber connector (Set and Twist).
Square, push-pull snap-in fiber connector (Subscriber/Square Connector).
Small Form Factor (SFF) push-pull fiber connector with retaining latch (Little/Lucent Connector).
Cable with fire-retardant fluoropolymer jacket emitting minimal smoke/non-toxic fumes; mandatory for air handling ducts and drop ceilings.
Standard polyvinyl chloride jacket cable; flexible and inexpensive but emits toxic chlorine gas when burned. Prohibited in plenum spaces.
An enclosed building area (above drop ceilings, below raised floors) used for environmental air distribution.
Signal interference caused by magnetic fields bleeding between adjacent wire pairs inside a cable.
Automatic Medium-Dependent Interface Crossover feature that automatically detects and configures proper cable connection type.
Standard memory module form factor used in desktop PCs, workstations, and servers with electrically independent pins on opposite sides.
Memory that synchronizes its bus timing with the CPU system clock for coordinated data transfers.
Memory technology that transfers data twice per clock cycle, on both rising and falling clock edges, doubling throughput.
Desktop DIMM: 240 pins; SO-DIMM: 204 pins; Voltage: 1.5V (1.35V Low Voltage); notch towards left center.
Desktop DIMM: 288 pins; SO-DIMM: 260 pins; Voltage: 1.2V; features curved contact edge for easier insertion.
Desktop DIMM: 288 pins; SO-DIMM: 262 pins; Voltage: 1.1V; includes on-module PMIC and dual 32-bit channels per module.
Memory controller communicates with all RAM over a single 64-bit bus (baseline memory bandwidth).
Two independent 64-bit channels (128-bit total throughput) using color-coded slots; requires matching pairs installed in specific slots.
Three independent memory channels (192-bit total throughput) found on high-end desktop and workstation platforms; requires modules installed in sets of 3.
Four independent memory channels (256-bit total throughput) standard on enterprise server/workstation platforms; requires modules installed in sets of 4.
Specialized memory that detects and corrects single-bit errors in real time; crucial for financial, scientific, and enterprise server environments.
Standard desktop memory lacking error detection and correction; inexpensive and suitable for general consumer PCs.
Standard memory where the memory controller directly addresses DRAM chips; offers lower latency for personal computers.
Memory with onboard register chip between DRAM and controller; reduces electrical load allowing servers to support large quantities of RAM.
Reserved disk space where inactive memory pages are moved to free up physical RAM when virtual memory is needed.
Operating system technique using secondary storage (HDD/SSD) as temporary memory when physical RAM is exhausted; significantly slower than DRAM.
Severe system slowdown caused by heavy reliance on virtual RAM, resulting in excessive disk I/O and poor overall performance.
Cloud service model delivering ready-to-use applications entirely over the web. CSP manages infrastructure; customer manages user access and configuration.
Pre-configured development and deployment environment in the cloud. CSP manages hardware/OS/database; developers manage custom code and data.
On-demand access to fundamental computing resources (VMs, storage, networks). CSP manages data centers; customer configures OS and applications.
Umbrella term for any service delivered over the cloud, including STaaS, NaaS, and SECaaS.
Cloud infrastructure owned and operated by a third-party CSP in multi-tenant environment on public internet; high scalability, low costs.
Cloud infrastructure dedicated exclusively to a single organization; hosted on-premise or off-site by third party; maximum control and privacy.
Combination of public and private cloud environments allowing data/applications to be shared between them based on business needs.
Shared cloud infrastructure used jointly by several organizations with common goals, security protocols, or compliance requirements.
Cloud characteristic allowing consumers to automatically provision computing capabilities without requiring human interaction with the provider.
Cloud characteristic enabling automatic scaling up or down of resources to handle changing workload demand in real-time.
The long-term capacity of cloud infrastructure to expand and handle growth in workload demand.
Cloud architecture where multiple separate customers (tenants) share the same physical server hardware while remaining logically isolated.
Cloud services where resource usage is monitored and billed based on actual consumption (bandwidth, CPU hours, storage volume).
Cloud offerings provided for a flat rate or fixed monthly fee regardless of actual consumption metrics.
Corporate desktop environments hosted on centralized virtual machines in a data center or private cloud, managed by enterprise administrators.
Cloud-hosted virtual desktops provided by third-party CSP on subscription basis, eliminating local server management.
Security framework defining which security tasks are managed by cloud provider vs. customer based on service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).
Standardized 6-step framework: Identify Problem → Establish Theory → Test Theory → Plan/Implement → Verify/Prevent → Document.
Gather information, examine the system, question the user, identify recent changes, perform backups, and review system logs.

term: Establish a Theory of Probable Cause (Step 2)
definition: Brainstorm potential causes using simplest explanations first; consider top-bottom/bottom-up approach or divide-and-conquer strategy.

term: Test the Theory to Determine Cause (Step 3)
definition: Validate hypothesis through targeted testing. If confirmed, proceed to Step 4. If disproved, establish new theory or escalate.

term: Establish a Plan of Action & Implement Solution (Step 4)
definition: Develop structured repair strategy, refer to vendor documentation, consider potential side effects, and execute the fix.

term: Verify Full System Functionality & Implement Preventive Measures (Step 5)
definition: Test thoroughly with end user, apply OS updates, install surge protectors, and implement policies to prevent future recurrences.
Log all details in ticketing system: record issue/root cause, solution steps taken, and update network documentation as needed.
Troubleshooting practice of checking basic physical connections and power settings before testing complex underlying components.
Troubleshooting approach that isolates problems by testing components halfway through system chain to determine which half contains the fault.
Transferring a technical issue to higher-level technician or specialized vendor when standard troubleshooting theories fail to produce resolution.
General-purpose desktop OS for business, gaming, enterprise domains. Supports Active Directory integration and extensive applications. Common editions: Home, Pro, Pro for Workstations, Enterprise.

Open-source OS used for servers, security tools, and development. Highly customizable with strong CLI tools. Wide distribution variety (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian). Used in web servers, penetration testing (Kali), and embedded systems.
Apple's workstation OS for Mac desktops and laptops. Known for tight hardware/software integration, strong multimedia workflows, and UNIX-based stability. Only runs on Apple hardware.

Lightweight cloud-centric OS built around the Chrome browser. Fast boot, low resource usage, ideal for education and web-based workflows. Limited offline capability; relies heavily on Google services.
Windows filesystem supporting permissions, encryption (EFS), compression, large file support, and journaling.
Maximum file size of 4 GB and maximum partition size of 2 TB. Used on legacy systems and removable drives.
Extensible File Allocation Table used for cross-platform removable storage. Supports large files; ideal for SD cards and USB drives.
Most common Linux filesystem. Features journaling, large volume support, stable and widely adopted.
Used on macOS, iOS, and iPadOS. Features snapshots, strong encryption, and optimization for SSDs.
Heavy posts preventing vehicle access. Used outside buildings to stop ramming attacks.
Two-door system controlling entry. Prevents tailgating and unauthorized access.
Uses RFID or NFC badges for controlled entry. Logs access events for audit trails.
Users receive only the access necessary to perform their job. Reduces risk of misuse or compromise.
Security philosophy that assumes no trust by default. Requires continuous authentication and authorization for all access.
Requires two or more authentication factors such as email, hardware token, authenticator app, SMS, voice call, TOTP, or OTP.
One login grants access to multiple systems. Reduces password fatigue and improves security.
Disguised as legitimate software. Delivers malicious payload once executed. Often used to install backdoors or steal data.
Hides processes, files, or system changes. Grants persistent, stealthy administrative access. Difficult to detect without specialized tools.
Encrypts files and demands payment for decryption. Can spread laterally across networks. Major business-impacting threat.
Monitors user activity. Captures browsing habits, keystrokes, or credentials. Often bundled with PUPs or malicious downloads.
Records keystrokes. Used to steal passwords, credit card numbers, and sensitive data.
Uses system resources to mine cryptocurrency. Causes performance degradation and high power usage.
Operates in memory without writing files to disk. Uses legitimate tools like PowerShell and WMI to avoid detection.
Real-time monitoring and behavioral analysis. Detects advanced threats like fileless malware. Provides automated response actions.
Outsourced security monitoring. Security analysts investigate alerts and respond to threats.

Sudden system crash with error code. Causes include faulty drivers, hardware failure, corrupt system files, overheating, or malware. Fix: Check Event Viewer, update drivers, run memory diagnostics, use sfc /scannow and DISM.

Slow apps, lag, freezing. Causes: too many startup apps, low RAM, malware, disk fragmentation, high CPU usage. Fix: Task Manager to identify heavy processes, disable startup apps, run malware scan, check disk health.
System File Checker command that scans and repairs corrupted system files in Windows.
Windows tool for repairing system image and component store corruption. Used alongside sfc for thorough system repairs.

Include user information, device information, issue description, category, severity level, escalation levels (Tier 1/2/3), clear written communication, progress notes, and issue resolution documentation.
Low (minor inconvenience), Medium (impacts productivity), High (critical system failure), Urgent (outage affecting multiple users).
Centralized database storing hardware details, software versions, network configurations, and relationships between systems.
Defines how to revert changes if issues occur. Must be tested, documented, and ready before implementation.
Testing changes in an isolated environment before production deployment. Prevents production impact and used for software updates, configuration changes, and new deployments.
Identifies responsible staff members including who performs the change and who approves the change before implementation.
Installing an OS from scratch without keeping previous data or settings. Recommended for fixing corrupted systems or major OS issues.
Upgrading to a newer OS version while keeping existing files, settings, and applications. Faster but carries more risk of conflicts.
A hidden system partition containing OS recovery tools and restore image data. Allows repair without external media.
Windows Pro/Enterprise encryption feature that encrypts entire drives. Requires TPM 2.0. Part of Windows security hardening.
Management tool for configuring Windows policies. Available in Pro/Enterprise editions. Not in Home edition.
Pro/Enterprise feature allowing remote access to PC. Home edition cannot host but can connect to others.
Enterprise-only feature that restricts which applications can run. Requires Group Policy to configure.
Shows running processes, performance metrics, and resource usage. Can end processes, adjust priority, and view network activity.
Manages hardware devices and drivers. Shows device status, allows driver updates/rollbacks, and disables devices.
Tool for managing partitions and volumes. Create/delete/resize partitions and extend volumes.
Displays system, security, and application logs. Shows errors, warnings, and informational events for troubleshooting.
Manages Windows services. Can start/stop/disable services and set startup type (Automatic/Manual/Disabled).
Monitors system performance counters in real-time. Shows CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics.
Advanced tool for editing Windows registry. Used for deep system configuration but risky if modified incorrectly.
Displays and manages IP configuration. ipconfig /all shows full details, /release /renew for DHCP, /flushdns clears cache.
Tests connectivity and latency to a host. Returns response time and packet loss statistics.
Queries DNS servers for hostname/IP resolution. Helps diagnose DNS failures and verify DNS configuration.
Shows active connections and listening ports. Useful for identifying suspicious network activity and open ports.
Traces the path packets take to reach a destination. Shows each hop and response times. Identifies routing issues.
Checks disk integrity and repairs errors. chkdsk /f fixes bad sectors, /r locates and marks bad areas.
Formats a drive with a specified filesystem. Example: format E: /fs:NTFS
Advanced disk partitioning tool. Creates/deletes partitions, converts MBR to GPT, cleans drives.
Robust file copy utility with multithreading and retry capability. Supports mirroring and logging.
System File Checker scans and automatically repairs corrupted Windows system files.
Refreshes Group Policy settings immediately without requiring a restart.
Windows security feature that prompts for admin consent before elevated operations. Can be disabled but reduces security.
Built-in firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic. Can create inbound/outbound rules.
Automatic OS and driver update mechanism. Critical for security patches and bug fixes.
Controls sleep, hibernate, and shutdown behavior. Affects battery life on laptops.
Configures resolution, refresh rate, scaling, and multi-monitor setup.
Manually configured IP address that doesn't change. Used for servers and devices requiring consistent access.
Automatic IP assignment from a DHCP server. Default for most client devices. Provides IP, gateway, DNS.
Translates hostnames to IP addresses. Can configure multiple DNS servers for redundancy.
Router address used to reach networks outside the local subnet. Critical for internet connectivity.
Encrypted tunnel to a remote network. Used for secure remote access and privacy.
Apple's modern filesystem with snapshots and encryption. Replaced HFS+.
macOS search tool for files, applications, and system settings. Accessed with Command+Space.
macOS backup utility that creates incremental backups to external drive. Can restore entire system or individual files.
macOS command-line interface using bash/zsh. Allows Unix commands and scripting.
Different Linux variants like Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian. Each has different package managers and tools.
Package manager used by Ubuntu/Debian. Syntax: apt install package-name
Package manager used by Red Hat/CentOS/Fedora. Syntax: yum install package-name
Runs commands with superuser privileges. Requires password confirmation. Essential for system administration.
Built-in antivirus and anti-malware protection. Automatically enabled and updated via Windows Update.
File-level access control allowing Read, Write, Execute permissions per user/group.
File-level encryption for NTFS. Different from BitLocker - encrypts individual files/folders.
Standard user (limited privileges) vs Administrator (full control). Security best practice: use Standard for daily work.
Enforced requirements for password complexity, minimum length, expiration, and history.
Latest wireless security standard with 192-bit encryption. Most secure option for home and enterprise networks.
Previous standard with 128-bit CCMP encryption. Still widely used and acceptable but less secure than WPA3.
Whether wireless network name is publicly visible. Hiding SSID adds minimal security - WPA3/WPA2 encryption is primary defense.
Allows/blocks specific MAC addresses. Easy to bypass but adds layer of access control.
Fraudulent emails/messages designed to steal credentials or deliver malware. Often impersonates banks or services.
Voice phishing via phone calls. Attacker impersonates authority (bank, IT support) to extract information.
SMS-based phishing. Text messages with malicious links or urgent requests to click/call.
Creating fictional scenario to gain trust and extract information. Example: posing as IT asking for password.
Following authorized person through secure door without credentials. Access control vestibules prevent this.
Offering something attractive (USB drive, download) to entice user to compromise security. Often contains malware.
1) Disconnect from network 2) Boot into Safe Mode 3) Run antivirus/anti-malware scan 4) Use specialized tools if needed 5) Restore from backup if necessary.
Boots Windows with minimal drivers and services. Used for troubleshooting and malware removal.
Dedicated anti-malware tool effective against spyware, PUPs, and advanced threats. Often used with traditional antivirus.
Configure inbound/outbound rules to block unnecessary traffic. Whitelist only required ports and services.
Turn off services not needed for daily operation. Reduces attack surface and improves performance.
Install security patches promptly. Unpatched software is primary attack vector for exploits.
At least 12 characters with uppercase, lowercase, numbers, special characters. Avoid dictionary words and personal info.
PIN, pattern, or biometric required to unlock device. Primary defense against physical theft.
Full-device encryption or app-specific encryption protects data if device is lost or stolen.
Mobile OSes restrict app access to camera, location, contacts, etc. Review and restrict when installing apps.
Developer feature allowing unauthorized device access. Should be disabled on user devices.
Encrypts entire storage device before recycling/disposal. Makes data unrecoverable even if drive is recovered.
Free tool that securely wipes drives by overwriting all data. Prevents data recovery.
Physically destroying storage media (shredding SSD, degaussing magnetic drives). Absolute security for sensitive data.
Biohazard label on equipment containing hazardous materials. Required for certified disposal.
Terminates unresponsive app without closing. Clears temporary cache and stops background processes.
Removes temporary app data improving performance. Different from Clear Data which removes all app info.
Standard restart of mobile device. Clears RAM and many temporary issues.
Factory reset wiping all data and apps. Returns phone to out-of-box state. Last resort for severe issues.
